questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Instantaneous Velocity and Acceleration
questions.q: If the velocity of a point mass is zero at a given instant, then its acceleration must also necessarily be zero at that same instant.
questions.hint: Think of a body thrown upwards at the highest point of its trajectory, or a harmonic oscillator at the extreme points of its motion.
explanations: Incorrect. Velocity can be instantaneously zero even if acceleration is non-zero (for example, when an object reverses its motion).

Correct! Velocity and acceleration are independent quantities. A body can have zero velocity and non-zero acceleration, such as a stone thrown into the air at the point of maximum height (where $v = 0$ but $a = -g$).

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Definition of Average Acceleration
questions.q: The average acceleration in a time interval is defined as the ratio between the total displacement and the time interval elapsed.
questions.hint: Remember the formula for average acceleration: does it involve the change in position or the change in velocity?
explanations: Incorrect. The ratio of displacement to time defines average velocity, not average acceleration.
Correct! Average acceleration is the ratio of the change in velocity to the time interval ($a_{avg} = \frac{\Delta v}{\Delta t}$). The ratio between displacement and time defines average velocity.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Position-Time Graph
questions.q: In uniform linear motion, the position-time graph is represented by a straight line whose slope corresponds to the velocity of the body.
questions.hint: The slope of a line in the $(t, x)$ plane indicates how much position $x$ changes as time $t$ changes.
explanations: Correct! The equation of motion for uniform linear motion is $x(t) = x_0 + v t$, which corresponds to the equation of a straight line in the $(t, x)$ plane with slope equal to velocity $v$.
Incorrect. The slope of the position-time graph precisely represents the velocity.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Sign of Acceleration and Velocity
questions.q: If the acceleration of a body is constant and non-zero, the magnitude of its velocity always increases over time.
questions.hint: What happens to the magnitude of velocity if velocity is positive but acceleration is negative?
explanations: Incorrect. If acceleration and velocity have opposite signs, the body slows down (the magnitude of velocity decreases).
Correct! The magnitude of velocity increases only if velocity and acceleration have the same sign. If they have opposite signs (for example, $v > 0$ and $a < 0$), the body is braking.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Geometric Meaning of the Velocity-Time Graph
questions.q: The area enclosed between the curve of the velocity-time graph and the time axis represents the displacement of the body in the considered time interval.
questions.hint: Think of the sum of the products $\Delta x_i = v_i \cdot \Delta t_i$, which geometrically equals the area under the curve.
explanations: Correct! In any velocity-time graph, the algebraic area enclosed between the curve $v(t)$ and the time axis corresponds to the total displacement $\Delta x$.
Incorrect. The geometric integration (area under the curve) of the velocity function with respect to time gives exactly the displacement.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Time Dependence of Displacement
questions.q: In uniformly accelerated linear motion, displacement varies linearly with time.
questions.hint: Examine the equation of motion for uniformly accelerated motion $x(t) = x_0 + v_0 t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2$.
explanations: Incorrect. The linear variation with time concerns velocity ($v = v_0 + a t$), not displacement.
Correct! In uniformly accelerated motion, displacement depends on the square of time ($t^2$), so it has a quadratic (parabolic) variation and not a linear one.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Definition of Instantaneous Velocity
questions.q: Instantaneous velocity corresponds to the limit of average velocity as the time interval approaches zero.
questions.hint: Consider the mathematical definition of the derivative of position with respect to time: $v(t) = \lim_{\Delta t \to 0} \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$.
explanations: Correct! Instantaneous velocity is defined precisely as the limit of the difference quotient $\frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ as $\Delta t \to 0$, which is the derivative of position with respect to time $v(t) = \frac{dx}{dt}$.
Incorrect. This is exactly the formal definition of instantaneous velocity.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Displacement and Average Velocity
questions.q: Average velocity in a time interval can be zero even if the body moved during that interval.
questions.hint: Think of a round trip where the end point coincides with the starting point.
explanations: Correct! If the final position coincides with the initial position, the net displacement is $\Delta x = 0$; consequently, the average velocity $v_{avg} = \frac{\Delta x}{\Delta t}$ is zero, regardless of the path traveled.
Incorrect. Average velocity depends solely on net displacement, which can be zero even when motion occurs.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Interpretation of the Velocity-Time Graph
questions.q: In a velocity-time graph $v(t)$, instantaneous acceleration at a given point is represented by:
questions.hint: Acceleration is the derivative of velocity with respect to time: $a = \frac{dv}{dt}$.
options: The slope of the line tangent to the curve at that point.
The height of the curve relative to the horizontal axis.
The area under the curve relative to the time axis.
explanations: Correct! Since acceleration is the first derivative of velocity with respect to time ($a = \frac{dv}{dt}$), on the $v(t)$ graph it corresponds to the slope of the line tangent to the curve.
Incorrect. The height of the curve represents the value of instantaneous velocity at that point.
Incorrect. The area under the curve represents the displacement of the body.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Vertical Free Throw Upwards
questions.q: An object is launched vertically upwards. Neglecting air resistance, at the point of maximum height:
questions.hint: The body stops for an instant before reversing direction, but the force of gravity continues to act without interruption.
options: The velocity is zero and the acceleration is directed downwards with magnitude $g$.
Both velocity and acceleration are zero.
Velocity is maximum and acceleration is zero.
explanations: Correct! At the highest point, the body reverses its motion, so its instantaneous velocity is $v = 0\text{ m/s}$. However, gravity continues to act constantly downwards; therefore, acceleration remains $a = -g \approx -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$.
Incorrect. If acceleration were also zero, the body would remain suspended in mid-air at the highest point without falling back down.
Incorrect. At the highest point, velocity is minimal (zero), not maximal.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Distinction Between Distance and Displacement
questions.q: Which of the following statements correctly describes the difference between distance traveled and displacement?
questions.hint: Displacement takes into account direction and final position relative to initial position, while distance calculates the total length of the trajectory.
options: Displacement is a vector quantity equal to the difference between final and initial positions, while distance traveled is a scalar that is always non-negative.
Displacement is always greater than or equal to distance traveled.
Distance traveled depends solely on the initial and final position of the body.
explanations: Correct! Displacement $\Delta x = x_f - x_i$ is a vector (in 1D it has a sign) that depends only on the end positions. Distance traveled $s$ is the total path length and is a scalar $s \ge 0$. It is always true that $s \ge |\Delta x|$.
Incorrect. The magnitude of displacement is always less than or equal to distance traveled ($|\Delta x| \le s$).
Incorrect. It is displacement that depends solely on the end positions, not distance traveled, which depends on the entire trajectory.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Time-Independent Equation of Motion
questions.q: In uniformly accelerated linear motion with initial velocity $v_0$ and acceleration $a$, what is the time-independent equation relating velocity, acceleration, and displacement $\Delta x$?
questions.hint: It is obtained by eliminating time $t$ from the system formed by $v = v_0 + a t$ and $\Delta x = v_0 t + \frac{1}{2} a t^2$.
explanations: Correct! Torricelli's equation $v^2 - v_0^2 = 2 a \Delta x$ (or $v^2 = v_0^2 + 2a \Delta x$) relates velocity, acceleration, and distance without needing to calculate time.
Incorrect. The formula is dimensionally incorrect (left side $\text{m/s}$, right side $\text{m}^3/\text{s}^2$).
Incorrect. The sign between the velocities must be minus, and there is a factor of 2 multiplying the acceleration.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Interpretation of the Signs of $v$ and $a$
questions.q: If the velocity of a point mass is negative ($v < 0$) and its acceleration is also negative ($a < 0$), the body is:
questions.hint: Compare the direction of motion with the direction of the applied force/acceleration.
options: Increasing the magnitude of its velocity (accelerating in the negative direction).
explanations: Correct! When velocity and acceleration have the same sign (in this case both negative), they work together: the body moves left/backward and increases the magnitude of its velocity.
Incorrect. The body slows down only when velocity and acceleration have opposite signs.
Incorrect. Velocity is constant only if acceleration is zero ($a = 0$).

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Concavity of the Position-Time Graph
questions.q: If the position-time graph $x(t)$ of a body is a parabola opening upwards, what can be deduced about the acceleration?
questions.hint: The concavity of the function $x(t)$ is determined by the sign of its second derivative $\frac{d^2x}{dt^2} = a$.
explanations: Correct! In the equation $x(t) = \frac{1}{2} a t^2 + v_0 t + x_0$, the upward concavity of the parabola indicates that the coefficient of the quadratic term is positive, so acceleration is positive ($a > 0$).
Incorrect. If acceleration were zero, the position-time graph would be a straight line.
Incorrect. If acceleration were negative, the parabola would open downwards.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Uniform Linear Motion
questions.q: A body moves in a straight line. If its instantaneous velocity is constant over a given time interval, which of the following statements is DEFINITELY CORRECT?
questions.hint: If velocity does not change over time, the change in velocity $\Delta v$ is zero.
options: The body's acceleration is equal to zero in the considered interval.
The body's displacement varies with the square of time.
The trajectory of the body must be circular.
Average acceleration is positive and non-zero.
The position of the body remains unchanged over time.
explanations: Correct! By definition, acceleration measures the change in velocity over time ($a = \frac{dv}{dt}$). If velocity is constant, $dv = 0$ and consequently acceleration is zero.
Incorrect. If velocity is constant, displacement varies linearly with time ($x = v t$).
Incorrect. The prompt specifies that it is a linear motion.
Incorrect. Average acceleration is zero because velocity does not change.
Incorrect. Position changes over time unless the constant velocity is equal to zero.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Acceleration due to Gravity
questions.q: In the free fall of a body near Earth's surface (setting the positive direction of the $y$-axis upwards and neglecting air resistance):
questions.hint: Acceleration due to gravity changes significantly only at large distances from Earth and always points toward the center of the planet.
options: Acceleration is constant and equal to $-g \approx -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ throughout the journey.
Acceleration increases as the body falls downward.
Acceleration changes sign when the body reverses its direction of motion.
Acceleration is zero at the point of maximum height.
The velocity of the body remains constant throughout the fall.
explanations: Correct! Near Earth's surface, acceleration due to gravity is constant and always directed downwards. With the axis pointing upwards, $a = -g \approx -9.8\text{ m/s}^2$ at every instant of motion (going up, at the stopping point, and going down).
Incorrect. Acceleration is considered constant for heights that are negligible compared to Earth's radius.
Incorrect. Gravity always pulls downward, so its sign never changes.
Incorrect. At the highest point, velocity becomes zero, not acceleration.
Incorrect. Velocity increases in magnitude downward due to constant acceleration.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Comparison Between Uniform and Accelerated Motion
questions.q: Consider two bodies A and B. Body A starts from rest at time $t = 0$ with constant acceleration $a$. Body B moves at constant velocity $v = a \cdot t_1$. At time $t = t_1$, what relation connects the displacements of the two bodies?
questions.hint: Calculate $\Delta x_A = \frac{1}{2} a t_1^2$ and $\Delta x_B = v \cdot t_1 = (a t_1) \cdot t_1$.
options: Body B has covered twice the distance covered by body A.
Body A and body B have covered the same distance.
Body A has covered twice the distance covered by body B.
Body A has covered four times the distance of body B.
It is not possible to determine without knowing the mass of the bodies.
explanations: Correct! Displacement of A is $\Delta x_A = \frac{1}{2} a t_1^2$. Displacement of B at constant velocity is $\Delta x_B = v \cdot t_1 = (a t_1) \cdot t_1 = a t_1^2$. Therefore, $\Delta x_B = 2 \Delta x_A$, meaning B covers twice the distance of A.
Incorrect. The two bodies would cover the same distance if they traveled at the same average velocity, but the average velocity of A is half that of B.
Incorrect. It is B that covered more distance because it traveled at maximum speed $a t_1$ for the entire time $t_1$.
Incorrect. The ratio between the two distances is 2, not 4.
Incorrect. In pure kinematics, the masses of the bodies do not affect the distance traveled.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Stopping Distance and Initial Velocity
questions.q: A car travels at speed $v_0$ and brakes with constant deceleration until it stops in a distance $S$. If the initial velocity were doubled to $2v_0$ with the same deceleration, the stopping distance would become:
questions.hint: Use Torricelli's formula $v^2 - v_0^2 = 2 a S$. With $v = 0$, $S = \frac{v_0^2}{2|a|}$.
explanations: Correct! From the formula $v^2 = v_0^2 - 2 a S$, setting $v = 0$ yields the stopping distance $S = \frac{v_0^2}{2a}$. If velocity doubles ($2v_0$), the distance becomes $S' = \frac{(2v_0)^2}{2a} = \frac{4v_0^2}{2a} = 4S$.
Incorrect. Stopping distance depends on the square of velocity, not directly proportional.
Incorrect. Stopping distance must increase as initial velocity increases.
Incorrect. The scale factor is $2^2 = 4$, not $2^3 = 8$.
Incorrect. $\sqrt{2}S$ would be obtained if velocity increased by a factor of $\sqrt{2}$.

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Calculating Acceleration via Derivative
questions.q: If the equation of motion of a point mass is described by the function $x(t) = C \cdot t^3$ (where $C$ is a positive constant), which expression represents the instantaneous acceleration $a(t)$?
questions.hint: Acceleration is the second derivative of position with respect to time: $a(t) = \frac{d^2 x}{dt^2}$.
explanations: Correct! The first derivative gives velocity: $v(t) = x'(t) = 3C t^2$. The derivative of velocity gives acceleration: $a(t) = v'(t) = 6C t$.
Incorrect. $3C t^2$ is the first derivative of position, which is instantaneous velocity $v(t)$.
Incorrect. $C$ is only the multiplicative constant present in the equation of motion.
Incorrect. $6C$ would be acceleration if the equation of motion were proportional to $t^2$.
Incorrect. Acceleration is zero only if position varies at most linearly with time ($t^1$).

questions.topic: Motion in One Dimension - Inflection Point on Position-Time Graph
questions.q: On a position-time graph $x(t)$ of linear motion, the presence of an inflection point indicates:
questions.hint: At the inflection point of the function $x(t)$, the second derivative $\frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$ changes sign and equals zero.
options: An instant at which instantaneous acceleration is zero and changes sign.
An instant at which the body's velocity becomes zero.
The instant at which the body reaches maximum displacement.
A point at which the body reverses its direction of motion.
A point at which velocity becomes infinite.
explanations: Correct! In calculus, an inflection point corresponds to the vanishing of the function's second derivative with a change in concavity. Since the second derivative of position with respect to time is acceleration ($a = \frac{d^2x}{dt^2}$), the inflection point indicates that acceleration is zero at that point and transitions from positive to negative (or vice versa).
Incorrect. Velocity becomes zero at stationary points (maxima, minima, or horizontal inflection points) where the first derivative $\frac{dx}{dt} = 0$.
Incorrect. Maximum displacement corresponds to a relative/absolute maximum point of $x(t)$.
Incorrect. Reversal of motion occurs when velocity changes sign ($v = 0$).
Incorrect. In classical physics, velocities are quantitatively finite and continuous.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Charge Conservation
questions.q: In an electrically isolated system, the total electric charge (algebraic sum of positive and negative charges) remains constant over time.
questions.hint: The principle of charge conservation states that charge is neither created nor destroyed, only transferred.
explanations: Correct! The law of conservation of electric charge is a fundamental principle of physics: in any process within an isolated system, the final net charge is always equal to the initial charge.
Incorrect. Electric charge in an isolated system is always conserved.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Charge Quantization
questions.q: The electric charge of any body can take on any continuous value.
questions.hint: Consider the microscopic nature of matter and the electron charge $e$.
explanations: Incorrect. Electric charge is not continuous but quantized.

Correct! Electric charge is quantized, which means that any observable charge in nature is always an integer multiple of the elementary charge $e \approx 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ ($Q = n \cdot e$).

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Conduction in Metals
questions.q: In metallic conductors, the motion of charge responsible for current or electrostatic rearrangement is due to the migration of protons.
questions.hint: Protons are bound inside atomic nuclei within the crystal lattice of the metal.
explanations: Incorrect. Protons are fixed in the atomic crystal lattice and do not move.
Correct! In metals, mobile charge carriers are solely conduction electrons (free to move), while protons remain bound in fixed atomic nuclei.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Charge Interaction
questions.q: Two electric charges with the same sign mutually attract each other with an electrostatic force.
questions.hint: Remember the fundamental rule of electrostatic interaction: like charges vs. opposite charges.
explanations: Incorrect. Charges of the same sign repel each other.
Correct! Charges of the same sign (like charges) repel, while charges of opposite signs attract each other.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Electrostatic Induction
questions.q: Electrification by electrostatic induction allows charges to be redistributed in a conductor without direct contact with the charged body.
questions.hint: Think of what happens when you bring a charged rod near an electroscope or conducting sphere without touching it.
explanations: Correct! Electrostatic induction occurs at a distance due to the force of the electric field that attracts or repels free charges in the conductor without physical contact.
Incorrect. Induction is precisely the phenomenon of redistribution at a distance without contact.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Units of Charge
questions.q: In the International System of Units (SI), the unit of measurement for electric charge is the Volt (V).
questions.hint: The Volt measures electric potential; what is the unit dedicated to electric charge?
explanations: Incorrect. The Volt is the unit of measurement for electric potential difference.
Correct! In the International System, electric charge is measured in Coulombs (C). The Volt (V) is the unit of measurement for electric potential.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Electrical Neutrality
questions.q: An electrically neutral body is a body with no electric charges inside it.
questions.hint: Atoms are composed of protons and electrons; what does it mean for total charge to be zero?
explanations: Incorrect. Matter contains an enormous number of positive and negative charges.
Correct! A neutral body contains a huge number of positive (protons) and negative (electrons) electric charges, but in perfectly equal numbers, ensuring a net total charge of zero.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Triboelectric Effect
questions.q: In electrification by friction, the material that becomes positively charged has gained protons from the other material.
questions.hint: Which subatomic particle has less mass and is located on the periphery of the atom?
explanations: Incorrect. Protons are not exchanged in ordinary friction phenomena.
Correct! During friction, only electrons are transferred. A body becomes positively charged when it gives up electrons, and negatively charged when it gains them.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Concept of Quantization
questions.q: What is meant by «quantization of electric charge»?
questions.hint: Electric charge always presents itself as a set of indivisible packets of value $e$.
options: Every isolated electric charge is an integer multiple of a fundamental elementary charge $e$.
Electric charge always increases continuously with temperature.
The electric charge of a body depends solely on its velocity.
explanations: Correct! Quantization establishes that the charge $Q$ of a body is always $Q = n \cdot e$, where $n$ is an integer and $e \approx 1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$ is the elementary charge of the electron.
Incorrect. Charge is not a continuous quantity.
Incorrect. Electric charge is an intrinsic property of matter that is invariant with respect to classical velocity.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Rubbing Glass and Silk
questions.q: When a glass rod is rubbed with a silk cloth, the rod acquires a positive electric charge. This occurs because:
questions.hint: Remember which particles move and in which direction during rubbing.
options: The rod gives up electrons to the silk cloth.
The rod gains protons from the silk cloth.
The rod loses neutrons to the silk cloth.
explanations: Correct! Glass has a lower electron affinity than silk, so during rubbing it gives up electrons to the silk. Having an electron deficit, the glass rod remains positively charged.
Incorrect. Protons are locked in nuclei and are not transferred by friction.
Incorrect. Neutrons carry no electric charge.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Electrification by Contact
questions.q: In the phenomenon of electrification by contact between a charged body and an initially neutral conductor:
questions.hint: Think of what happens to the charge when two conductors touch, sharing electrons.
options: Part of the charge transfers to the neutral conductor, which acquires a charge of the same sign as the charged body.
The neutral conductor always acquires a charge of the opposite sign to that of the charged body.
There is no transfer of electrons between the two bodies.
explanations: Correct! During contact, like charges on the charged body repel each other and part of them passes to the neutral conductor. As a result, the conductor gets charged with the same sign as the original body.
Incorrect. Electrification by contact always provides charges of the same sign (unlike temporary induction).
Incorrect. There is an actual flow of electrons between the touching bodies.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Elementary Charge
questions.q: What is the approximate numerical value of the elementary charge $e$ (magnitude of electron charge)?
questions.hint: It is a fundamental constant on the order of $10^{-19}\text{ C}$.
explanations: Correct! The elementary charge $e$ is approximately $1.602 \times 10^{-19}\text{ Coulombs}$.
Incorrect. $9.109 \times 10^{-31}\text{ kg}$ is the mass of the electron, not its charge.
Incorrect. $8.854 \times 10^{-12}\text{ F/m}$ is the vacuum permittivity $\varepsilon_0$.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Induction in a Neutral Conductor
questions.q: What happens inside a neutral conductor when a negatively charged body is brought near it without touching it?
questions.hint: The free electrons of the conductor are repelled by the nearby negative charge.
options: The free electrons of the conductor move toward the far side, leaving the near side positively charged.
The electrons of the conductor are attracted toward the side near the charged body.
The entire conductor instantly becomes permanently negatively charged.
explanations: Correct! Due to the repulsive electrostatic force, free electrons (negatively charged) migrate to the side furthest from the charged body. The near side is left with an excess of positive charges (uncompensated protons).
Incorrect. Electrons are repelled by the negative charges of the external body, not attracted.
Incorrect. The total charge of the isolated conductor remains neutral; only the local charge distribution changes.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Conductors and Insulators
questions.q: What is the fundamental microscopic difference between a conductor and an insulator (dielectric)?
questions.hint: The difference lies in the freedom of movement of the atom's outermost electrons.
options: In conductors, outer electrons are free to move throughout the material; in insulators, they are tightly bound to individual atoms.
Conductors contain only protons, while insulators contain only electrons.
In insulators, electrons do not exist, while in conductors only free positive charges exist.
explanations: Correct! In conductors (such as metals), valence electrons form a "gas of free electrons". In insulators (such as glass, plastic, wood), all electrons are tightly bound to their respective atomic nuclei.
Incorrect. Both conductors and insulators are composed of atoms made of protons, neutrons, and electrons.
Incorrect. All stable materials contain electrons.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Calculating Number of Electrons
questions.q: An initially neutral body has a final net charge of $Q = +4.8 \times 10^{-18}\text{ C}$. Knowing that the elementary charge is $e = 1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}$, how many electrons did the body lose?
questions.hint: Use the charge quantization formula $Q = N \cdot e \implies N = \frac{Q}{e}$.
explanations: Correct! $N = \frac{Q}{e} = \frac{4.8 \times 10^{-18}\text{ C}}{1.6 \times 10^{-19}\text{ C}} = 30$. Having a positive charge, the body lost $30$ electrons.
Incorrect. Error by a factor of $10$ in dividing powers of ten.
Incorrect. $3$ corresponds to $\frac{4.8}{1.6}$, but ignores proper handling of $10^{-18}$ and $10^{-19}$ exponents.
Incorrect. $48$ is just the numerical mantissa value without dividing by the electron charge.
Incorrect. $16$ is derived incorrectly from the value of $e$.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Charge Distribution Between Identical Spheres
questions.q: Consider three identical conducting spheres A, B, and C. Initially A has charge $+Q$, B has charge $-2Q$, and C is neutral ($0$). Sphere C is first brought into contact with sphere A and then separated. Next, sphere C is brought into contact with sphere B and separated. What is the final charge of sphere C?
questions.hint: When two identical conducting spheres touch, total charge is distributed equally between them.
explanations: Correct! 1) Contact A and C: total charge $+Q + 0 = +Q$. Dividing equally, C and A get $q_C = +\frac{Q}{2}$. 2) Contact C and B: total charge $+\frac{Q}{2} + (-2Q) = -\frac{3}{2} Q$. Dividing equally between B and C, each gets $q_{C,fin} = \frac{1}{2} \left(-\frac{3}{2} Q\right) = -\frac{3}{4} Q$.
Incorrect. This would be obtained if C had zero charge before the second contact with B.
Incorrect. Algebraic sign error in summing charges between C and B.
Incorrect. Omission of equal charge division during the second contact.
Incorrect. Sphere C acquires and transfers charge in each conductive contact.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Law of Conservation of Charge
questions.q: Which of the following statements accurately describes the law of conservation of electric charge?
questions.hint: Analyze the behavior of the algebraic sum of charges in a closed system.
options: In an isolated system, the algebraic sum of positive and negative charges does not change over time.
The total charge of a body increases indefinitely as temperature increases.
In collisions between subatomic particles, total electric charge always becomes zero.
The overall electric charge of the universe varies depending on chemical reactions.
Two conducting bodies brought into contact always zero out their total charge.
explanations: Correct! The principle states that in any electrically isolated system, the net amount of charge remains strictly constant.
Incorrect. Temperature does not create or destroy net electric charge.
Incorrect. In subatomic reactions total charge is conserved, not zeroed out.
Incorrect. The charge of the universe is constant; chemical reactions only involve reorganizing electrons.
Incorrect. On contact, charges redistribute, but their sum remains unchanged.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Polarization of Dielectrics
questions.q: When a charged body is brought near a neutral insulator (e.g., bits of paper), the insulator is attracted. How is this phenomenon explained?
questions.hint: In insulators, electrons do not move freely, but charges within molecules undergo a slight shift (dipoles).
options: By polarization: the molecules of the insulator align/deform, creating a surface charge of opposite sign near the charged body.
By conduction: electrons from the insulator jump directly onto the attracting charged body.
By Joule effect: the insulator heats up and creates air suction toward the charged body.
By complete induction: the insulator becomes an ideal conductor that transfers charge to the air.
By gravity: the charge of the body increases the atomic mass of the paper pieces.
explanations: Correct! The presence of the charged body induces polarization of the dielectric: electrons in the insulator's molecules shift slightly, orienting atomic dipoles. The charge of the opposite sign is closer to the charged body, overriding the repulsive force and producing net attraction.
Incorrect. In insulators, electrons cannot move freely or jump from one body to another simply by proximity.
Incorrect. The Joule effect refers to heating due to electric current flow.
Incorrect. An insulator does not become a conductor under ordinary electrostatic conditions.
Incorrect. The interaction is purely electrostatic and not gravitational.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Coulomb's Law
questions.q: According to Coulomb's law, how does the electrostatic interaction force between two point charges $q_1$ and $q_2$ vary as their distance $r$ changes?
questions.hint: Examine the dependence on $r$ in the formula $F = k_0 \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$.
options: The force is inversely proportional to the square of the distance ($1/r^2$).
The force is directly proportional to the distance ($r$).
The force is inversely proportional to the distance ($1/r$).
The force is independent of distance $r$.
The force is directly proportional to the square of the distance ($r^2$).
explanations: Correct! Coulomb's law states that the magnitude of electrostatic force is $F = k_0 \frac{|q_1 q_2|}{r^2}$, so it decreases inversely with the square of the distance between charges.
Incorrect. If it were directly proportional to $r$, the force would increase as charges move further apart.
Incorrect. It depends on the square of distance $r^2$, not simple distance $r$.
Incorrect. Distance significantly affects the magnitude of electrostatic force.
Incorrect. Inverse dependence, not direct.

questions.topic: Electrostatics - Charge Equilibrium Between Conductors
questions.q: Two identical isolated conducting spheres have charges $q_1 = +8\,\mu\text{C}$ and $q_2 = -2\,\mu\text{C}$. If they are brought into contact and then separated again, what will be the final charge on each sphere?
questions.hint: Calculate the total charge on the system $q_{tot} = q_1 + q_2$ and divide it equally between the two identical spheres.
explanations: Correct! The total charge of the system is $q_{tot} = (+8\,\mu\text{C}) + (-2\,\mu\text{C}) = +6\,\mu\text{C}$. Since the two conducting spheres are identical, upon contact the charge distributes uniformly: each sphere will have $q = \frac{+6\,\mu\text{C}}{2} = +3\,\mu\text{C}$.
